A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same HWC-Loco research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and revised experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original terrain-navigation, embodiment and disturbance experiments in Tables 1–3, alongside policy-sensitivity analyses and real-robot demonstrations.

after.justification: v3 reports original locomotion, disturbance and expressive-motion experiments in Tables 1–4, plus observation-history experiments and additional real-robot demonstrations.

M1.justification: The goal-tracking and ZMP-based recovery policies, Double-DQN selector, Wasserstein imitation objective and VAE estimator are retained. Expressive-motion experiments explicitly reuse the training pipeline. Added VAE specifications and recovery-reward explanations disclose implementation details without establishing a changed control procedure.

E1.justification: v3 adds punching, dancing and expressive-walking tasks, outdoor locomotion including grassy surfaces, and outdoor disturbance scenarios. Simulated robustness coverage changes from maintaining a standing posture under directional impulses to locomotion under forces, CoM impulses and payloads. CMU locomotion data and the H1/G1 embodiments remain.

E2.justification: v3 Table 4 adds a domain-randomized Motion-tracking policy as the comparator for expressive-motion tasks. DreamWaQ, AHL, Goal-tracking Policy and HWC-Loco-l remain in corresponding locomotion comparisons. ExBody and ExBody2 supply methodological references, rather than separately evaluated baseline rows.

E3.justification: Section 5 changes the human-likeness metric from MSE to Wasserstein-1 distance. Robustness evaluation now uses commanded locomotion over uniformly mixed terrains, with specified force durations, CoM-velocity perturbation ranges and 0–5 or 0–10 kg payloads. Appendix A.8 adds evaluations at history lengths 1, 10, 20 and 40. The retained terrain benchmark still uses 1200-step evaluations.

E4.justification: v3 substantially broadens recovery stress testing from standing impulses to disturbances during locomotion, including persistent forces and payloads. It adds observation-history sensitivity analysis (Table 14), outdoor disturbance cases and a punching-recovery case study (Figure 14). Existing saliency and extreme-state distribution analyses are retained and relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report training with three random seeds and use ± values and graphical variability displays. v3 extends these practices to additional results without documenting increased replication, a new uncertainty estimator, confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: For the matched high-speed stair setting, HWC-Loco success changes from 88.72 ± 0.42% to 84.34 ± 0.43%, while goal tracking changes from 0.99 ± 0.03 to 1.07 ± 0.03 (v1 Table 2; v3 Table 1). Separate flat/obstacle results disappear, standing-disturbance results are replaced, and new disturbance, motion-tracking and history-length results appear. Human-likeness values use different metrics and cannot be compared directly.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 corrects the discriminator's stated codomain from {0,1} to R, consistent with its Wasserstein-critic formulation. The POMDP definitions, robust optimization formulation, ZMP mathematics and duality discussion otherwise remain. Combining and renumbering equations does not introduce new theory.

C1.justification: Both versions claim hierarchical whole-body control that balances task tracking and safety recovery across terrains, embodiments and deployment environments. v1's conclusion already claims applicability beyond locomotion; v3's expressive-motion experiments provide new support for that retained claim.

C2.justification: v3 adds explicit limitations concerning fixed low-level controllers and discrete switching, the deployed robot's 19 DoFs, and incomplete realism of simulated recovery disturbances. It also adds interpretations linking G1 performance to mass and joint flexibility, long observation histories to reduced adaptability, and motion-recovery behavior to sacrificing tracking for stability.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies VAE architecture and hyperparameters, PPO activation, recovery-policy velocity-error tolerances, RTX 4090 training hardware and per-policy training costs. It also documents JIT export and deployed model sizes, supplies additional robot specifications, and adds a project-page link. These are substantial disclosures; they do not establish corresponding changes to the original implementation.

R1.justification: v3 expands related work with simulated-avatar control and newer humanoid systems including ASAP, TWIST and AMO, and adds ExBody2 and disturbance-testing references. It removes the Tan et al. hierarchical-controller and Double-Q-learning references. The central positioning around recovery from safety-critical situations remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is reorganized: policy sensitivity moves into Section 4.3, embodiment evaluation moves into the scalability section, and real-world terrain discussion joins effectiveness evaluation. Appendix methods are reordered and experiments divided into H1/G1 subsections. Several passages are tightened or rewritten; an explicit limitations section is added and the Impact Statement removed.

P2.justification: The two-column main text becomes predominantly single-column, with a redrawn framework overview and an opening recovery illustration. Tables are restructured, and VAE, history-length, motion-tracking and robot-configuration displays are added. New outdoor and motion-recovery figures accompany relocated existing demonstrations; the policy-sensitivity plot also changes its displayed iteration range.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for the central robustness claim by evaluating recovery during locomotion under persistent forces, impulses and payloads, beyond v1's quantified standing-disturbance test. Expressive-motion comparisons directly support the previously asserted extension beyond locomotion. The history ablation, implementation disclosures and explicit limitations further improve assessability. These gains outweigh losing separate flat/obstacle results, although the new motion-tracking protocol remains sparsely specified.
